The Managing Director of NG Clearing Limited, Farooq Oreagba, has opened up about his battle with an incurable form of cancer, revealing that he is currently undergoing treatment and expects to return to remission in 2027. Oreagba, 60, said the condition was detected during a medical screening on February 4, adding that his treatment was progressing well. He disclosed this in an interview with TheCable Lifestyle on Monday, noting that despite the diagnosis, he had continued working and pursuing his usual activities. “I have an incurable form of cancer. It comes, I treat, and it goes. I was diagnosed in February, after which I rode at Ojude Oba, celebrated my 60th and continued as if nothing was wrong,” he said. “I am very fine, working as usual and doing what I always do. My treatment is going well, and I expect to be back in remission by March/April next year.” Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Add us to your Preferred Sources Oreagba, who is popularly known as the ‘King of Steeze’, came into the national spotlight in 2024 after his appearance at the Ojude Oba Festival in Ijebu-Ode, Ogun State, went viral. His fashionable outfit and confident display on horseback during the annual cultural celebration of the Ijebu people drew widespread attention, making him a prominent figure on social media. But behind the public attention, Oreagba has been dealing with cancer for more than a decade. He was diagnosed with bone marrow and skin cancer in February 2014, a development that temporarily took him away from his career. He underwent a transplant in August 2014. United Nigeria airline partners cancer society to fund screening, treatment 10 Nollywood stars who battled cancer before deaths Ikeja Club marks 60th anniversary with free cancer, hypertension screening The businessman, who has been receiving treatment in Johannesburg, South Africa, described the condition as one he has learnt to manage and said it had not prevented him from going about his daily life. He also used his experience to encourage Nigerians to take routine medical screening seriously, stressing that early detection was important in managing cancer. According to him, the disease was identified following a screening exercise he underwent on February 4. He said he undergoes checks every three months and recommended that people should have regular medical examinations. “As you can see from my posts, I am still doing what I have always done, and nothing will change,” he said. “I was detected early, on the back of a screening that I did on 4th Feb. The message is simple… early detection saves lives, and I recommend regular checks. I do mine every three months, but even every six months would suffice.” Oreagba further urged people not to regard a cancer diagnosis as an automatic death sentence, saying his progress showed that it was possible to continue living while managing the illness. “It is important to know that a cancer diagnosis is not a death sentence. I am making great progress,” he added. “I am and will remain a testament that a cancer diagnosis is NOT a death sentence.” The investment banker has always been vocal about his experience with cancer, and how it had reshaped his outlook on life, saying he had come to see the diagnosis differently.
